content: The individual described is a retired farmer who was once very hard-working. Despite his retirement, he remains active and engaged in various physical activities to maintain his independence. His weekly routine includes a variety of activities: Monday, Wednesday, and Friday: He participates in a 30-minute community class designed for seniors. Tuesday and Thursday: He spends 15 minutes walking, often to the market, and also engages in house cleaning. Saturday: He dedicates 30 minutes to fishing and another 30 minutes to swimming in the river. Sunday: He spends 15 minutes gardening and attends a 60-minute community class for seniors. The guidelines emphasize that any level of physical activity is beneficial, and individuals who are not currently active should start small and gradually increase their activity levels. Regular physical activity is important for everyone, regardless of age, weight, or health condition. Adults with chronic diseases or disabilities are encouraged to consult a healthcare professional or physical activity specialist to determine the most suitable types and amounts of activity for their needs. Additional equipment or support may be necessary for individuals with disabilities. It is also recommended to limit sedentary behavior. Replacing sedentary time with any form of activity, even light-intensity movement, can provide health benefits. For children under one year of age, no screen time is advised, and they should not be restrained for more than one hour at a time. Good-quality sleep, including naps, is essential, with recommended durations varying by age group: Under 1 year: 12–17 hours of sleep. 1–2 years: 11–14 hours of sleep with naps and a regular schedule. 3–4 years: 10–13 hours of sleep with naps and a regular schedule. 5–17 years: Adequate good-quality sleep is essential, with limited screen time, especially sedentary screen time. Adults (18–64 years) and older adults (65+ years): Adequate good-quality sleep is recommended, and sedentary time should be minimized. Safety considerations for physical activity include starting slowly and gradually increasing intensity and duration to avoid injuries. Warming up before and cooling down after moderateto vigorous-intensity activities is important. Reflective clothing should be worn when walking at night, and individuals should dress appropriately for the weather, including wearing proper footwear, hats, sunscreen, and insect repellent. Vigorous outdoor activities should be done in the morning or evening to avoid the midday sun, and staying hydrated by drinking water is essential. A safe environment for physical activity should always be prioritized. For individuals with medical conditions, increasing physical activity is generally beneficial but should be approached with caution. Adults and older adults with chronic conditions such as cardiovascular disease, hypertension, or type 2 diabetes may need to consult their healthcare provider to determine the appropriate types and amounts of activity based on their individual needs, abilities, and limitations. Pre-exercise medical clearance is usually unnecessary for those without contraindications who are beginning lightor moderate-intensity activities, such as brisk walking or daily living tasks. Stretching should only be done after muscles are warmed up. These recommendations are supported by global and regional guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep, which highlight the importance of regular movement for physical and mental health.
